flashcards.q: What transformation is allowed in bronze, and what's the most common mistake teams make there?
flashcards.a: Bronze: raw, immutable, append-only, near-source shape, no business logic, no joins, no dedup. The common mistake is applying 'just a little' cleaning (trimming whitespace, casting types) because it seems harmless — it destroys bronze's ability to distinguish a source bug from a transformation bug during an incident.

flashcards.q: What belongs in silver vs. gold?
flashcards.a: Silver: cleaning, type enforcement, deduplication, conforming entities across sources, surrogate key assignment, SCD application, referential integrity — still near source grain. Gold: grain declared explicitly, dimensional modeling, aggregation, business-rule definitions, deliberate denormalization.

flashcards.q: Why must bronze be immutable and append-only even though it costs more storage?
flashcards.a: It's the only layer that can reconstruct full history if a bug is found in silver/gold logic months later. You can always rebuild downstream from bronze, but never reconstruct bronze from a layer that already discarded raw detail.

flashcards.q: Compare Kimball, Inmon, and Data Vault on time-to-first-value and consumption-readiness.
flashcards.a: Kimball: fast time-to-value, directly BI-ready. Inmon: slow (integrated EDW built first), not directly BI-ready, needs a mart layer. Data Vault: moderate speed (hubs/links added quickly), not directly BI-ready, also needs a mart layer on top.

flashcards.q: What's the honest, current synthesis on Kimball vs Inmon vs Data Vault for a large regulated organization?
flashcards.a: Hybrid by layer, not one methodology for the whole warehouse: a Data Vault or Inmon-style normalized integration core for governance/historization/audit, feeding Kimball-shaped marts as the consumption layer for BI ergonomics.

flashcards.q: What is a late-arriving dimension, and what pattern fixes it?
flashcards.a: A fact event references a dimension entity not yet loaded (fact and dimension pipelines run at different latencies). Fix: insert an inferred-member placeholder row (natural + surrogate key, null attributes) so the FK isn't dangling; update it in place (Type 1) when real data arrives.

flashcards.q: A gold fact table's row count triples after a routine dimension refresh. What's the likely cause?
flashcards.a: The gold join matches a Type 2 dimension on the natural key with no as-of/effective-date filter, so the fact row joins against every historical version of that entity instead of just the version correct at the time — fan-out.

flashcards.q: Why must surrogate key generation happen after deduplication, not in bronze?
flashcards.a: Bronze can contain multiple raw representations of the same logical entity (duplicate CDC events, or two source systems' records before conforming). Assigning surrogate keys before resolution produces distinct keys for what should be one entity, propagating into every downstream fact's foreign key.

flashcards.q: Why is deliberate denormalization safe in gold but dangerous in an OLTP schema?
flashcards.a: OLTP point-updates rows constantly, so denormalization's update anomalies are a real correctness risk. Gold is read-heavy and rebuilt/merged on a schedule rather than point-updated, so the update-cost side of the tradeoff is largely a non-issue while the read-simplicity benefit is constant.

flashcards.q: Why should analysts not query a Data Vault's hub/link/satellite structure directly for BI?
flashcards.a: The Vault is optimized for auditability and historization, not query ergonomics — reconstructing 'what a dimension currently looks like' requires joining across many satellite tables per query. A Kimball mart on top does that reconstruction once and exposes a denormalized, BI-friendly star schema.

flashcards.q: Two dashboards show different 'revenue' numbers. What's the likely root cause and the structural fix?
flashcards.a: Ad hoc queries bypassing governed gold tables/marts and re-deriving 'revenue' with slightly different filter/join logic. Fix: consolidate the definition into one gold table or semantic-layer metric, and restrict direct query access to bronze/silver for anything feeding an external number.

flashcards.q: When is the medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture overkill?
flashcards.a: For a small warehouse with one source system and a handful of tables — three layers of transformation for data that could be cleaned and aggregated in one pass is process overhead without payoff.

flashcards.q: How does dbt map onto the medallion layers?
flashcards.a: dbt's staging/ layer roughly maps to silver's cleaning step, intermediate/ and marts/ map to gold. dbt snapshot automates Type 2 SCD mechanics; dbt tests/contracts enforce the layer boundaries.
